items.title: Byte streams vs character streams
items.context: InputStream/OutputStream handle raw bytes (e.g. images, any binary data). Reader/Writer handle characters and understand text encoding — the right choice when working with text files.

questions.prompt: Which pair of classes is designed for reading and writing text with proper character encoding?
questions.explanation: Reader/Writer operate on characters and handle encoding/decoding; InputStream/OutputStream work at the raw byte level.

questions.prompt: Why is try-with-resources commonly used when working with file streams?
choices: It automatically closes the resource (calls close()) even if an exception is thrown
It makes I/O run on a background thread automatically
It disables checked exceptions for I/O
It converts byte streams into character streams
questions.explanation: Any resource implementing AutoCloseable (like FileInputStream) gets close() called automatically at the end of the try block, exception or not — avoiding leaked file handles.

items.title: Java NIO: Channels & Buffers
items.context: The classic java.io API is stream-based and blocking. java.nio introduces Channels (a connection to a source/destination, e.g. a file or socket) and Buffers (a fixed-size container you read from/write into), enabling non-blocking, more efficient I/O for high-throughput scenarios.

questions.prompt: Which two abstractions are central to Java NIO?
questions.explanation: NIO is built around Channels (the connection to a data source) and Buffers (the data container you read into or write from) — a different model from classic stream-based I/O.

questions.prompt: You're building a server that needs to handle many concurrent connections efficiently. Why might NIO be a better fit than classic java.io streams?
choices: java.io cannot read files larger than 2GB
NIO removes the need for a network at all
NIO supports non-blocking I/O, so one thread can manage many channels instead of one thread per connection
questions.explanation: Classic streams block a thread per connection; NIO's non-blocking channels + selectors let a small number of threads multiplex many connections, which scales far better under high concurrency.

items.title: Serialization
items.context: Serialization converts an object's state into a byte stream (for storage or transmission); deserialization reconstructs the object from that stream. A class must implement java.io.Serializable to be eligible.

questions.prompt: Which interface must a class implement to be serializable in Java?
choices: Externalizable is required, Serializable is optional
questions.explanation: java.io.Serializable is a marker interface (no methods) that tells the JVM this class's instances may be converted to and from a byte stream.

questions.prompt: What does marking a field `transient` do during serialization?
choices: Excludes it from the serialized byte stream
Makes it the only field that gets serialized
questions.explanation: transient fields are skipped during serialization (e.g. passwords or derived/cacheable data) and come back as their default value (null/0/false) after deserialization.

items.title: Path & Files (NIO.2)
items.context: Since Java 7, java.nio.file.Path represents a file system path (replacing much of java.io.File's role), and the static Files utility class provides methods like readAllLines, copy, move, and exists.

questions.prompt: Which class represents a file system path in the modern NIO.2 API, largely superseding java.io.File?
questions.explanation: java.nio.file.Path (introduced in NIO.2, Java 7) is the modern representation of a file system path, used together with the Files utility class.

questions.prompt: Which class provides static utility methods like Files.readAllLines() and Files.copy()?
questions.explanation: java.nio.file.Files is a utility class of static methods for common file operations — reading, writing, copying, checking existence — operating on Path objects.

items.title: Networking I/O: sockets
items.context: Socket is used for a client-side TCP connection to a server; ServerSocket listens for and accepts incoming TCP connections on the server side. Together they're the foundation of Java's blocking network I/O.

questions.prompt: Which class does a Java client use to open a TCP connection to a server?
questions.explanation: Socket represents one end of a two-way TCP connection from the client's perspective, connecting to a given host and port.

questions.prompt: Which class does a Java server use to listen for and accept incoming TCP connections?
questions.explanation: ServerSocket binds to a port and blocks on accept(), returning a new Socket for each incoming client connection.

items.title: Buffered streams
items.context: Wrapping a raw stream/reader (e.g. FileReader) in a BufferedReader/BufferedWriter batches reads and writes into an internal buffer, drastically reducing the number of expensive underlying I/O system calls.

questions.prompt: Why commonly wrap a FileReader in a BufferedReader?
choices: It changes the file's encoding automatically
It reduces the number of costly underlying I/O calls by reading in larger internal chunks
It's required — FileReader cannot be used directly
questions.explanation: Without buffering, each read can trigger a system call; BufferedReader reads a larger chunk into memory at once and serves subsequent reads from that buffer, which is far more efficient.

items.title: Bridging byte and character streams
items.context: InputStreamReader and OutputStreamWriter are bridge classes that convert a byte stream into a character stream (and back), applying a specified character encoding — the connective tissue between java.io's byte and character worlds.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of InputStreamReader?
choices: It reverses the order of bytes in a stream
It converts a byte stream into a character stream, decoding bytes using a given (or default) charset
It duplicates a stream into two copies
questions.explanation: InputStreamReader wraps a raw InputStream and decodes its bytes into characters according to a charset, bridging byte-oriented and character-oriented I/O.

items.title: NIO.2: checking and watching files
items.context: Files.exists()/Files.notExists() check a path without throwing on absence. WatchService (NIO.2) lets an application register a directory and receive events when files inside it are created, modified, or deleted, instead of polling.

questions.prompt: Which NIO.2 method checks whether a file exists at a given Path, without throwing if it doesn't?
questions.explanation: Files.exists(path) returns a boolean, making existence checks straightforward without needing to catch an exception.

questions.prompt: What does NIO.2's WatchService let an application do?
choices: Receive notifications when files in a watched directory are created, modified, or deleted
questions.explanation: WatchService lets you register a directory and be notified of file system change events as they happen, avoiding the need to repeatedly poll the directory yourself.

items.title: File attributes
items.context: The Files utility class also exposes file metadata: size, last-modified time, and whether a path is a directory or a regular file, without needing to open the file's contents.

questions.prompt: Which method tells you whether a given Path refers to a directory rather than a regular file?
questions.explanation: Files.isDirectory(path) (and its counterpart Files.isRegularFile(path)) checks the path's type without reading its contents.

questions.prompt: Which method retrieves a file's last-modified timestamp?
questions.explanation: Files.getLastModifiedTime(path) returns the file's last-modified time as a FileTime, one of several metadata attributes exposed without opening the file's content.

items.title: Closeable vs AutoCloseable
items.context: AutoCloseable (the broader, general-purpose interface used by try-with-resources) declares close() as throwing any Exception. Closeable extends it, narrowing close() to only throw IOException and requiring it be safely callable multiple times (idempotent).

questions.prompt: What's a key difference between java.io.Closeable and java.lang.AutoCloseable?
choices: Closeable cannot be used with try-with-resources
AutoCloseable is only for network resources
Closeable narrows AutoCloseable's close() to only throw IOException, and requires it be safely callable more than once
questions.explanation: Closeable extends AutoCloseable specifically for I/O resources: its close() is restricted to throwing IOException (not any Exception) and is expected to be idempotent — calling it again after the resource is already closed should be a harmless no-op.

questions.prompt: A try-with-resources statement declares two resources, A then B. If both open successfully, in what order are they closed?
choices: B then A — reverse of declaration order
Both are closed simultaneously on separate threads
A then B, same as declaration order
questions.explanation: try-with-resources closes resources in the reverse of the order they were declared/opened — the last one acquired is the first one released, mirroring how you'd naturally unwind nested resources.

items.title: DataInputStream & DataOutputStream
items.context: DataInputStream/DataOutputStream read and write Java's primitive types (int, double, boolean, ...) in a portable binary format, letting you serialize primitive values without hand-rolling byte-level encoding.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of DataOutputStream/DataInputStream?
choices: Automatically converting text between character encodings
Writing and reading Java primitive types in a portable binary format
questions.explanation: DataOutputStream provides methods like writeInt()/writeDouble()/writeBoolean() that encode primitives in a well-defined binary layout, and DataInputStream reads them back symmetrically with readInt()/readDouble()/readBoolean().

items.title: Object serialization streams
items.context: ObjectOutputStream and ObjectInputStream serialize and deserialize entire Java objects (implementing Serializable) to and from a byte stream, handling the object graph — including nested objects — automatically.

questions.prompt: Which pair of classes serializes and deserializes whole Java objects (not just primitives) to and from a stream?
questions.explanation: ObjectOutputStream.writeObject()/ObjectInputStream.readObject() serialize and reconstruct entire object graphs, following references to nested objects automatically, as long as every class involved implements Serializable.

items.title: Reading input with Scanner
items.context: Scanner parses primitive types and strings out of an input source (like System.in, a file, or a String) using configurable delimiters, making simple text parsing much less verbose than manually working with streams and readers.

questions.prompt: What is Scanner commonly used for?
choices: Parsing primitive values and tokens (words, numbers) out of a text input source like System.in
questions.explanation: Scanner wraps an input source and provides convenient methods like nextInt(), nextLine(), and hasNext() to tokenize and parse text without manually handling byte/character streams.

items.title: Selectors and multiplexed I/O
items.context: A Selector (java.nio.channels) lets a single thread monitor many channels at once for readiness events (readable, writable, connectable) instead of dedicating one thread per connection — the foundation of scalable non-blocking network servers.

questions.prompt: What role does a Selector play in Java NIO?
choices: It lets one thread monitor multiple channels for readiness (read/write/connect) instead of needing one thread per channel
It automatically compresses files being read
It encrypts data flowing through channels
It converts byte channels into character channels
questions.explanation: A Selector is registered with multiple channels and reports which ones are ready for an operation, letting a small number of threads efficiently multiplex a large number of concurrent connections — the mechanism behind highly scalable non-blocking servers.

items.title: Memory-mapped files
items.context: MappedByteBuffer (via FileChannel.map()) maps a file's contents directly into memory, letting you read/write it as if it were an in-memory array — the OS handles paging data in and out, which can be much faster than explicit read()/write() calls for large files.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of memory-mapped file I/O (MappedByteBuffer)?
choices: It lets a program access file contents as if they were in memory, letting the OS manage paging, often faster for large files than explicit reads/writes
It's required to read any file larger than 1KB
questions.explanation: Memory mapping avoids repeated explicit read/write system calls by letting the OS's virtual memory system handle bringing pages of the file into memory on demand, which is typically much faster for large files accessed non-sequentially.

items.title: Copying files with NIO.2
items.context: Files.copy(source, target) throws FileAlreadyExistsException if the target already exists, unless you pass the StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING option to explicitly allow overwriting.

questions.prompt: What happens calling Files.copy(source, target) when target already exists, without any copy options?
choices: It appends source's content to target
It renames target automatically before copying
questions.explanation: Files.copy() is deliberately conservative by default and refuses to overwrite an existing file unless you explicitly pass StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING.

items.title: URL & URLConnection
items.context: URLConnection (obtained via url.openConnection()) represents a communication link to a resource identified by a URL — commonly used to fetch content over HTTP before higher-level HTTP client libraries existed, and still available as a lightweight built-in option.

questions.prompt: Which method obtains a connection to a resource identified by a URL object?
questions.explanation: URL.openConnection() returns a URLConnection (or a more specific subtype like HttpURLConnection) representing the link to that resource, which you can then use to read its content or headers.

questions.prompt: What does HttpURLConnection let you inspect that a plain byte stream from a file wouldn't provide?
choices: HTTP-specific details like the response status code and headers
The database schema used by the server
The exact CPU that served the request
questions.explanation: HttpURLConnection exposes HTTP semantics — response codes, headers, request methods — on top of the underlying byte stream, since it's modeling an HTTP exchange rather than a plain file.

items.title: Buffer capacity, limit and position
items.context: A NIO Buffer tracks three key values: capacity (the fixed maximum it can hold), limit (the boundary past which you shouldn't read/write in the current mode), and position (the next index to read or write). limit can never exceed capacity.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a Buffer's capacity and its limit?
choices: Capacity changes as you read and write; limit never does
Capacity is the buffer's fixed maximum size; limit is the current boundary for reading/writing, which can never exceed capacity
Limit is always larger than capacity
questions.explanation: Capacity is fixed once the buffer is allocated — it's the size of the underlying array. Limit marks how much of that capacity is currently usable for the buffer's active mode (reading or writing), and by definition can never be set higher than capacity.

questions.prompt: What does a Buffer's position represent?
choices: The index of the next element that will be read or written
A fixed marker that never changes
The total number of bytes ever written to it
questions.explanation: position tracks where the next get() or put() will read from or write to; it advances automatically as you read/write and is reset by operations like flip() and rewind().

items.title: flip() switches a Buffer from writing to reading
items.context: After writing data into a Buffer, calling flip() sets its limit to the current position and resets position to 0 — preparing the buffer to be read back from the beginning, up to exactly the data that was written.

questions.prompt: Why do you call buffer.flip() after writing data into it and before reading it back?
choices: flip() clears all the data in the buffer
flip() sets the limit to the current position and resets position to 0, switching the buffer from write mode to read mode over exactly what was written
flip() is only needed for direct buffers
flip() reverses the byte order of the data
questions.explanation: Without flip(), attempting to read would start from wherever the write left position (near the end, past the real data) — flip() repositions to the start and caps the limit at exactly how much was actually written.

items.title: Types of NIO channels
items.context: FileChannel reads/writes files. SocketChannel and ServerSocketChannel handle TCP client connections and server listening, respectively. DatagramChannel handles UDP packets. All can be used in blocking or non-blocking mode.

questions.prompt: Which NIO channel type is used for reading and writing files?
questions.explanation: FileChannel is specifically for file I/O; SocketChannel/ServerSocketChannel handle TCP networking, and DatagramChannel handles connectionless UDP packets.

items.title: Blocking vs non-blocking I/O
items.context: In blocking I/O, a thread calling read()/write() waits until the operation completes before doing anything else. In non-blocking I/O (NIO's core value proposition), a thread can initiate an operation and immediately move on to other work, checking back (or being notified via a Selector) once it's ready.

questions.prompt: What is the defining characteristic of non-blocking I/O?
choices: It's always faster for every workload
A thread doesn't have to wait for a read/write to complete before doing other work
It eliminates the need for a network connection
questions.explanation: Non-blocking I/O lets a thread kick off an operation and immediately go do something else — rather than sitting idle until the read/write finishes — which is what allows a small number of threads to service many concurrent connections via a Selector.

items.title: Direct vs heap buffers
items.context: ByteBuffer.allocate() creates a heap buffer, backed by a regular JVM byte array. ByteBuffer.allocateDirect() creates a direct buffer, backed by native (off-heap) memory — allocation is more expensive, but I/O operations on it can be faster since the OS can access that memory directly, without an extra copy into a native buffer first.

questions.prompt: What's the main trade-off of a direct (allocateDirect()) ByteBuffer compared to a regular heap buffer?
choices: Direct buffers are always slower to use for I/O
Direct buffers are more expensive to allocate but can make I/O operations faster by letting the OS access the memory without an extra copy
Direct buffers cannot be used with FileChannel
questions.explanation: Direct buffers live outside the normal JVM heap, so the OS can read/write them without the JVM first copying data into a native-friendly buffer — faster for I/O-heavy code, but allocation/deallocation cost more than a simple heap array.

items.title: Zero-copy transfer between channels
items.context: FileChannel.transferTo()/transferFrom() can move data directly between two channels (e.g. a file and a socket) using the operating system's own zero-copy mechanisms, avoiding the extra round trip of copying bytes into a Java buffer and back out.

questions.prompt: What performance benefit does FileChannel.transferTo() offer when copying a file's contents to a socket?
choices: It can let the OS transfer data directly between the file and the socket, avoiding extra copies through a Java buffer
It runs the transfer on multiple threads automatically
It encrypts the data in transit
questions.explanation: transferTo()/transferFrom() can take advantage of OS-level zero-copy support, moving bytes directly between the source and destination without staging them through a user-space Java buffer — a common optimization for serving files over a network.

items.title: Character encoding pitfalls
items.context: Opening a file with a Reader/Writer that doesn't explicitly specify a Charset relies on the JVM's platform default encoding — which can differ between operating systems and configurations, causing subtly corrupted text (mojibake) when code runs somewhere with a different default than where it was written and tested.

questions.prompt: Code that reads a text file works fine on the original developer's machine but produces garbled characters when deployed elsewhere. What's a likely cause?
choices: Text files cannot be read cross-platform
The code relied on the JVM's platform default charset instead of explicitly specifying one, and the two environments have different defaults
questions.explanation: Without an explicit Charset (e.g. StandardCharsets.UTF_8) passed to the Reader/Writer, Java falls back to the platform's default encoding — which can silently differ between machines/OS configurations, a classic source of environment-dependent encoding bugs.

items.title: Flushing buffered output
items.context: Data written to a BufferedOutputStream (or BufferedWriter) sits in memory until the internal buffer fills up, flush() is called explicitly, or the stream is closed — relying on data being 'written' without one of those happening can mean it never actually reaches the underlying destination.

questions.prompt: Why might data written to a BufferedOutputStream not appear in the underlying file immediately?
choices: Buffered streams write instantly and this can't happen
The data sits in an internal buffer until it fills up, flush() is called, or the stream is closed
It only applies to network streams, not files
questions.explanation: Buffering exists precisely to batch up small writes into fewer, larger underlying I/O operations — which means data can sit unflushed in memory until the buffer fills, you call flush() explicitly, or the stream closes.

items.title: Path normalization and resolution
items.context: Path.resolve(other) joins a path with another (relative) one. Path.normalize() removes redundant elements like "." and ".." without touching the file system. Path.isAbsolute() tells you whether a path is already fully qualified from the file system root.

questions.prompt: What does Path.normalize() do?
choices: Converts a relative path into an absolute one by checking the file system
Removes redundant path elements like "." and ".." purely as a string/path operation, without touching the file system
Deletes the file at that path
questions.explanation: normalize() is a purely syntactic cleanup of the path string itself — collapsing '.' and resolving '..' segments — it doesn't check whether the resulting path actually exists on disk.

items.title: try-with-resources close order

questions.prompt: What is the order of the printed lines?
questions.explanation: Resources declared in a try-with-resources header are closed in the reverse of their declaration order — B was declared last, so it's closed first, then A. This mirrors how you'd unwind nested resources manually in old try/finally code.

items.title: FileReader on a missing file
items.context: FileReader reader = new FileReader("does-not-exist.txt");

questions.prompt: What happens when this line runs, if the file doesn't exist?
questions.explanation: The classic java.io FileReader/FileInputStream constructors throw the checked FileNotFoundException (a subclass of IOException) when the file can't be opened for reading. The newer java.nio.file API (Files.newInputStream, etc.) instead throws NoSuchFileException for a missing path — a common point of confusion when mixing old and new I/O.

items.title: BufferedReader EOF behavior

questions.prompt: What does the second readLine() call return?
questions.explanation: BufferedReader.readLine() signals end-of-stream by returning null, not by throwing an exception. This trips people up coming from Scanner, whose next()/nextLine() throw NoSuchElementException at EOF instead — two different I/O idioms for the same situation.

items.title: Scanner.nextInt() on non-numeric input
items.context:
Scanner sc = new Scanner("abc");
int n = sc.nextInt();

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
questions.explanation: Scanner.nextInt() peeks at the next token and throws InputMismatchException if it doesn't match an integer's lexical pattern — the token is left unconsumed. This is distinct from Integer.parseInt("abc"), which throws NumberFormatException.

items.title: Serializing a class with a non-serializable field

questions.prompt: What happens when writeObject() runs?
choices: Serializes fine; dbConnection is skipped automatically
Throws IOException with no further detail
Throws NotSerializableException naming the Connection class
questions.explanation: Java serialization walks every non-transient, non-static field. Config itself implements Serializable, but its dbConnection field references a class that doesn't — so writeObject() throws NotSerializableException identifying the offending class. Marking the field `transient` is how you tell serialization to skip it.

items.title: transient fields after deserialization

questions.prompt: What does this print after deserialization?
questions.explanation: Fields marked transient are deliberately excluded from serialization — their value is never written out. On deserialization, a transient field is left at its type's default (null for objects, 0/false for primitives), regardless of what it held before serialization. Non-transient fields like user round-trip normally.

items.title: InputStream.read() at end of stream

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: InputStream.read() (the no-arg, single-byte overload) returns the byte read as an int in the range 0-255, or the sentinel value -1 to signal end-of-stream — it does not throw when there's simply nothing left to read. EOFException exists but is used by higher-level APIs like DataInputStream's readInt(), not the base read().

items.title: Suppressed exceptions in try-with-resources

questions.prompt: Which exception propagates out of the try-with-resources statement, and what happens to the other one?
choices: Only "close failed" propagates; the body exception is lost
Both propagate as two separate uncaught exceptions
"body failed" propagates, with "close failed" attached as a suppressed exception
Only "body failed" propagates; "close failed" is discarded entirely
questions.explanation: When both the try block and an implicit close() throw, try-with-resources propagates the original body exception as the primary one, and attaches the close-time exception to it via addSuppressed() — retrievable later with getSuppressed(). This preserves the more meaningful root cause instead of silently swallowing it, which is exactly the behavior of legacy try/finally that try-with-resources was designed to fix.

items.title: Files.readAllLines on a missing path
items.context:
Path path = Path.of("missing-dir/missing-file.txt");
List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(path);

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs, if the path doesn't exist?
questions.explanation: The java.nio.file API consistently uses NoSuchFileException (a subclass of IOException) for a missing path, unlike the older java.io classes which throw FileNotFoundException. Mixing the two APIs in the same codebase is a common source of catch-clause bugs.

items.title: Calling close() twice

questions.prompt: What happens on the second call to close()?
choices: Silently does nothing — close() is idempotent for most streams
questions.explanation: Closeable's contract explicitly allows close() to be called more than once, and most JDK stream implementations honor this by making the second (and later) calls a no-op rather than throwing. This is precisely what makes try-with-resources safe even when you also close a resource manually inside the block.
